title: John of God (8 March)
hook: a former soldier and bookseller who began caring for the sick, and whose followers became a hospital order

segments.voice: Yesterday, Casimir, the prince who turned his army around and gave his money to the poor. Your line was the prince who refused. Which fight did you turn down? Day nine hundred seventy-three.

A street in Granada, in Spain. A man who sells holy books and pictures from a little shop stands in a crowd listening to the preacher John of Avila. Something in the sermon breaks him open. He runs through the streets shouting, crying out for mercy, tearing up his own books, giving away everything in the shop. The neighbors decide he has lost his mind. So he is taken to the city hospital and locked in the ward for the mad. That ward is where today's story really begins. His name was John, and the Church calls him John of God.
screen: `A BOOKSELLER IN GRANADA.` → `A SERMON BREAKS HIM OPEN.` → `LOCKED IN THE WARD FOR THE MAD.`

segments.voice: Before Granada, tradition says, John had been a shepherd, a soldier and a drifter. None of it had gone well. Now he was inside the hospital, and he saw what was done there to people judged insane. On that ward, tradition says, the treatment was beating, to drive the madness out. John was beaten too. And he made a decision, there on the ward: if he ever got out, he would care for the sick the way he wished someone had cared for him and the men beside him. John of Avila came to visit him and calmed him, and when John was released, he did exactly that. He rented a house, filled it with the sick and the homeless, and went out at night with a basket, begging for them. Tradition says his cry in the streets was, roughly, do good, brothers, to yourselves, meaning that helping the poor was a gift to the giver. He washed patients, carried them on his back, and sorted them by need. The bishop, tradition says, gave him the name John of God. After his death his helpers carried on, and became the Hospitaller Brothers of Saint John of God, a religious order devoted to the sick. In the Douay-Rheims, Jesus describes the judgment, and the kindnesses done to him in the least of people: "sick, and you visited me: I was in prison, and you came to me." John had been both. A man who had been treated as mad became a patron of hospitals and the sick.
screen: `SHEPHERD, SOLDIER, DRIFTER, BOOKSELLER.` · `BEATEN ON THE WARD FOR THE MAD.` · `A RENTED HOUSE AND A BASKET AT NIGHT.` · `HIS HELPERS BECOME AN ORDER.` · then, large: `SICK, AND YOU VISITED ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: fill John's basket. Settle, and breathe. Picture him at night in Granada, going door to door with an empty basket for the sick in his rented house. Now bring to mind one person you know who is ill, or worn out caring for someone who is. Ask what would actually go in a basket for them. Not flowers. Soup. A lift to an appointment. Their bins taken out. An hour so the carer can sleep. Choose one thing and put it in the basket. If you pray, you can pray for that person and the people who care for them. If you don't, just keep them in mind with your breathing. The bell holds the time.
Granada, the Spanish city where John of God, once locked up as mad, began caring for the sick, and whose helpers became the Hospitaller Brothers.

Your line: the hospitaller. A week of saints: two brothers and an alphabet, the martyrs of Libya, the Fatima children, a blunt monk, a prayer from the depths, a prince who turned back, and now John. Today, call or visit someone who is sick. Day nine hundred seventy-three.

howItsDone: Catholics keep 8 March as the memorial of Saint John of God, patron of hospitals, nurses and the sick, and the Hospitaller Order he inspired runs hospitals and care homes that mark the day with Mass and celebrations for patients and staff.
